newsitem.title: USA: Ill. school funding plan vote expected Friday.
newsitem.headline: Ill. school funding plan vote expected Friday.

text.p: Illinois House Speaker Michael Madigan has set a vote Friday on an education funding plan that would provide $600 million of new revenues for schools and finance a $2 billion school construction bond program.
Madigan late Wednesday outlined the basics of the proposal, which closely follows Illinois Gov. Jim Edgar's education funding plans in most respects, spokesman Steve Brown said.

Edgar, a Republican, and Madigan, a Democrat, have both proposed a 25 percent state income tax increase from 3 percent to 3.75 percent to finance education funding reforms that would provide property tax cuts and increased school revenues.
Under the Madigan plan, the projected $1.5 billion generated by the income tax increase would provide $900 million of property tax cuts and $600 million of school funding, Brown said.

Another $100 million of revenues from projected state growth would also be split out to finance the issuance of $2 billion of school construction bonds for a matching program with local districts, Brown said.
Taken altogether, the proposal could provide $4 billion of school construction to Illinois schools, Brown said.
The bond program "has always been something the speaker and a lot of house democrats have felt strongly about and, frankly, a lot of people in suburban Chicago areas too," Brown said.
"He's always thought that if we were really going to get into the fundamental change in education funding that this would be a critical component," Brown said.
Edgar has proposed $600 million for schools and $1.2 billion of property tax cuts, but his plan also has a $340 million gap.
The Madigan proposal also includes teacher accountability issues now under discussion with the Illinois Education Association and the Illinois Federation of Teachers, Brown said.
"The details on those have not really been finalized," Brown said.
Madigan hopes for substantial support from representatives of both parties, Brown said.
"Regardless of party or geographical region, everyone has been talking about a need for fundamental change in the way we fund schools," Brown said.

Both plans have the intent of raising per-pupil spending to a minimum of $4,225 in all Illinois districts. Neither plan would reduce aid to more affluent districts, some of which spend more than $15,000 per student.
Edgar's plan has run into opposition from within his own party, where House Minority Leader Lee Daniels has questioned the proposed 25 percent income tax hike.

Daniels has proposed a lesser income tax increase combined with other taxes to raise base funding for less affluent districts over two years and phase in property tax relief over six years, spokesman Brian Timpone said.
Lawmakers hope to finish their session Friday and adjourn with a budget for fiscal 1998, which begins on July 1.
